items.title: Remote Sensing for Division B
items.text:
An outline of the official rules is here

This competition consists of two parts.

Roughly 1/3rd of the points scored will focus on remote sensing in general:

  • Understanding the Electromagnetic Spectrum
  • Sensors
  • Satellite orbits
  • Instrumentation
  • Image Characteristics

The remaining 2/3rd of the points will focus on interpreting data from specific missions:

  • How to use/interpret maps in general
  • Implications for Earth

items.title: Remote sensing concepts (25-35% of total points) . .
items.text:
A. Properties of light: electromagnetic spectrum, reflection, refraction, absorption, scattering, polarization, irradiance and radiance

B. Types of sensors, limited to: (1) Passive: optical and thermal sensing in the ultraviolct, visible, near-infrared, shortwave infrared, and thermal infrared ranges ; (2) Active: radar backscatter, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), interferometric SAR (InSAR) data basic interpretive level, radar altimetry, and radar-derived elevation products

C. Types of satellite orbits and their purposes, limited to: low earth, medium earth, high canh, polar: non-polar, geostationary, geosynchronous ;

D. Image characteristics: spatial, temporal, radiometric (limited to signal-to-noise ratio/ sensitiv; } and spectral resolution

E. Instrumentation, limited to: scanning systems, multispectral imaging systems, optical and infrared imagers, radiometers, radar altimeters, thermal infrared imagers, synthetic aperture radar (SAR) instruments, and digital elevation models

items.title: Interpretation and analysis of remote sensing images and data sets.
items.text:
This topic will be limited to the types of sensors listed in Section 1, Part B. Questions will be drawn from the following satellites only:

  • Different spectral combinations from Landsat 5-9 (TM. ETM, OLI)
  • Sentinel-lA/1B, Sentinel 2A/2B,
  • Terra (limited to: MODIS. ASTER),
  • Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM)
  • ECOSTRESS
  • GOES

Questions will focus on the following:

A. Fundamentals of mapping as applied to topographic maps, satellite images, aerial photographs, and other maps generated by remotely sensed data

1. Marginal information: location, date, scale, orientation, legend, labels, etc.

2. Image display and interpretation: natural color, false color, grayscale, thermal, radar, elevation,

contours, classified map displays

3. Measurements and scaling estimates, limited to: distance between features, perimeter, area,

altitude, elevation, slope

B. Earth observation and monitoring 

1. Physical phenomena, including but not limited to:
    a. Absorption and scattering by aerosols and their effect on data collection
    b. Albedo, surface temperature, reflectance, and other properties of natural and engineered materials and their uses for classifying land areas
    c. Elevation or subsidence changes
    d. Vegetation changes (e.g., forests, agriculture)
    e. Geohazards: canoes, landslides, flooding, wildfires
    f. Earth processes: glacial movement, fluvial processes, stream patterns

2. Land Cover Classification Systems
    a. Supervised and unsupervised classification maps
    b. National Land Cover Database (NLCD/CONUS) Land Cover Change Index

3. Human and environmental implications: 
    a. habitat loss 
    b. land cover change
    c. urbanization
    d. deforestation
    e. damage assessment 
    f. monitoring

items.title: Instrumentation for Remote Sensing Satellites
items.text:
Most remote sensing satellites typically have instruments with one of two types:

  1. Passive Radiometers, i.e., devices that measure

  2. uv, optical and near-infrared light that has been emitted by the sun and is reflected by the Earth, and /or

  3. mid-infrared (aka "thermal infrared) light that is emitted by the Earth,

These imaging data are used to monitor fires and floods, evolution of ice caps, plant growth and/or urban sprawl.

  1. Active Radiometers (aka radar), that emit radio-wavelength signals toward the earth and measure the time it takes for the reflected signals to return the satellite.

  2. radar altimeters

  3. SAR instruments and associated digital elevation models

Besides providing consistent "3D" maps of the whole earth, these data are also used to measure the height of large tracts of the ocean, glaciers, earthquake-racked areas.

To get the highest possible spatial resolution and widest possible coverage on each orbit depends on the particular scanning technique.

items.title: title: Instrumentation
items.text:

It will also describe the characteristics of radar-equipped satellites, particularly their distinguishing characteristics.

items.text:
1. Satellites with optical and/or infrared instruments use

  2. pushbroom scanning

  5. Stripmap

  6. ScanSAR

items.text:
This topic includes:

  • physical phenomena

items.title: Mapping Fundamentals
items.text:
Interpretation of the maps, including:

  • the map "meta-data", e.g., location and data
  • map display types, e.g., natural or false color, topographic
  • quantitative measurements from maps, e.g., distance between or areas of features

The types of maps to be interpreted include:

  • satellite images, e.g. optical and infrared cameras
  • topographic maps, generated by RADAR mapping satellites
  • Aerial photography (which of the missions generates aerial photography)?
  • other types of maps generated by combining satellite images and topographic maps

items.title: Orbits for Remote Sensing Satellites
items.text:
Satellites used for Remote Sensing are in one of these types of orbits:

Orbit Type a.k.a. Altitudes (km) Oribtal Periods Low Earth Orbit LEO 160 km to 2000 km 1.55 hr. -- 2.13 hr. Medium Earth Orbit MEO 2000 km to 35,786 km 2 hr. -- <24 hr. High Earth Orbit HEO >= 35,786 km 1 day

Use an LEO for a mission that requires high spatial resolution (without having to engineer and pay for a very large telescope).

Use an HEO for a mission that requires continuous monitoring of some point on Earth.

MEO's have neither of the above advantages, and are not often used for remote sensing. However, they do offer an advantage for satellite missions that require wide area coverage, such as communications (e.g. Starlink) or surveillance purposes.

items.title: foo
items.text: Q: How does NASA classify satellite orbits? A: There are 3 common classes of satellite orbits:

items.title: Common types of orbits
items.text:
Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) : Altitudes from 160 to 2,000 km above Earth. Used for crewed stations and the NASA Earth Observing System fleet because close proximity allows high-resolution data collection.

Medium-Earth Orbit (MEO) : Altitudes from 2,000 to 35,500 km. Used utilized for navigation and GPS constellations.

High-Earth Orbit (HEO) : Altitudes above 35,500 km. Used for continuous weather and broad communication monitoring.

items.title: Sub-types of HEO orbits
items.text:
Geosynchronous (GSO) & Geostationary (GEO): : Orbits at 35,786 km where orbital speed matches Earth's rotation. Geostationary paths stay fixed directly over the equator, hovering over the exact same spot continuously.

Geosynchronous paths cover a range of latitudes above and below the equator;
they appear over the same spot at the same time each day.

Sun-Synchronous Orbit (SSO): : A specific near-polar path where the orbital plane precesses at the same rate as the Earth moves around the Sun, ensuring consistent shadow and lighting conditions for scientific imaging.

Polar Orbit: : Passes nearly directly over both geographic poles (90-degree inclination), allowing global coverage over time as the planet rotates underneath.

Highly Elliptical / Molniya Orbits: : Elongated paths spending maximum dwell time over targeted high-latitude regions.

Orbit Type Altitude Range(km) Orbital Peiods Applications LEO 180-2000 1.5-2 hours Remote Sensing MEO 2000-35000 a few-several hours Navigaton; GPS HEO 35786 1 day However over a single point (Geostationary), or Range of latitudes at the same time each day
